claims.text: FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers possess compositional complexity and severe atomic-scale lattice distortion.
The starting multilayers possess or are predisposed to chemical short-range order.
Sustained loading produces progressive time-dependent plastic deformation in these multilayers.
Creep is governed primarily by the combined action of interface-mediated dislocation pile-ups and mechanically induced short-range-order evolution.
Changing nanoscale layer thickness alters local lattice distortion near multilayer interfaces.
Changing compositional gradients alters local lattice distortion near multilayer interfaces.
Layer-thickness and composition-induced changes in lattice distortion tune the balance between dislocation accumulation and MSRO evolution, thereby tuning creep rate.
Multilayer interfaces restrict dislocation nucleation and motion.
Interfacial restriction of dislocations localizes strain in regions adjacent to the interfaces.
Localized deformation and crystalline lattice defects can trigger or modify mechanically induced short-range order.
Short-range order alters nonuniform lattice strain fields and dislocation behavior in multi-principal-element alloys.
Evolving MSRO can harden the material by stabilizing dislocation obstacles or soften it when the order is disrupted.
Thicker layers will produce more pronounced dislocation pile-ups and a higher creep rate than the baseline.
Compositional gradients that reduce MSRO stabilization will increase creep rate relative to the baseline.
Promoting robust MSRO at interfaces will reduce dislocation mobility and creep rate relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the nanoscale multilayer architecture remains preserved.
The proposed mechanism ceases to dominate if phase transformations or diffusion-dominated creep become controlling.
Changes in loading conditions can shift the dominant creep mechanism.
The quantitative contributions of dislocation pile-ups and MSRO evolution to creep rate are uncertain.
Failure of layer-thickness and composition variations to produce significant or systematic changes in creep rate, dislocation pile-ups, and MSRO evolution would falsify the proposed mechanism.
